body:
Religious diversity within sacred landscapes

A multi-faith sacred landscape contains religious buildings, practices or historical associations belonging to more than one religious tradition. Such landscapes may develop through centuries of settlement, pilgrimage, trade and interaction between communities.

Religious diversity can take different forms. Several religious traditions may maintain separate shrines within the same geographical area, or followers of different religions may visit a common shrine. These situations should not be treated as identical.

Examples within major pilgrimage centres

  • Girnar: Contains important Hindu and Jain pilgrimage sites, including the Neminatha Temple, Amba Mata Temple, Dattatreya shrine and Bhavnath Mahadev Temple.
  • Palitana: The sacred Jain landscape of Shatrunjaya also contains the shrine of Angar Pir, a Muslim saint remembered in local tradition.
  • Champaner-Pavagadh: Contains Hindu shrines, Jain temples and Islamic religious architecture from different historical periods.
  • Bet Dwarka: Its religious heritage includes Krishna worship and a Sikh gurdwara associated with Bhai Mohkam Singh, one of the Panj Pyare.

The Panj Pyare were the 5 beloved disciples initiated by Guru Gobind Singh at the establishment of the Khalsa in 1699.

Islamic pilgrimage traditions

A dargah is a shrine centred on the tomb of a Muslim religious figure, particularly a Sufi saint. The devotional visit to such a shrine is called ziyarat. Historically, some Sufi shrines have attracted visitors from different religious and social backgrounds.

Haji Pir Dargah

Haji Pir Dargah is situated in Kutch district. It is associated with the worshipful remembrance of the Muslim saint Haji Pir. Its annual religious gathering attracts devotees from both Hindu and Muslim communities, making it an important example of shared pilgrimage heritage.

Sarkhej Roza

Sarkhej Roza, near Ahmedabad, is an important Islamic architectural and religious complex associated with the Sufi saint Shaikh Ahmad Khattu Ganj Bakhsh, who was connected with the reign of Sultan Ahmad Shah I.

The complex includes the saint's tomb, a mosque, royal structures and a large historic water tank. It combines religious, architectural and historical significance.

Zoroastrian and Sikh religious heritage

Udvada

Udvada, in Valsad district, is an important pilgrimage centre of the Parsi Zoroastrian community. It houses the Iranshah Atash Behram, one of the most revered sacred fires of the community.

Atash Behram denotes the highest grade of consecrated fire in the Zoroastrian religious tradition. The fire temple is associated with the preservation and continuity of Parsi religious heritage in Gujarat.

Lakhpat

Lakhpat, in Kutch district, contains a historic Sikh gurdwara associated with the travels of Guru Nanak. A gurdwara is a Sikh place of worship centred on reverence for the Guru Granth Sahib.

Jain and Buddhist heritage at additional sites

Taranga

Taranga Hill in Mehsana district is an important Jain pilgrimage centre. Its principal historic Jain temple is dedicated to Ajitanatha, the second Tirthankara, and is associated with the 12th-century Chaulukya period.

The surrounding landscape also contains archaeological remains associated with Buddhism.

Dev Ni Mori

Dev Ni Mori, near Shamlaji in Aravalli district, is an important Buddhist archaeological site. Excavations revealed remains of a stupa and a relic casket. A stupa is a sacred Buddhist monument commonly associated with relics or commemoration of the Buddha and Buddhist religious figures.

Dev Ni Mori illustrates Gujarat's historical Buddhist heritage. Its archaeological significance should be distinguished from the continuing ritual pilgrimage associated with active shrines such as Ambaji or Dwarkadhish Temple.

Prelims focus

  • Haji Pir Dargah, Kutch, represents shared Hindu-Muslim pilgrimage heritage.
  • Sarkhej Roza is associated with Shaikh Ahmad Khattu Ganj Bakhsh.
  • Udvada, Valsad, is associated with the Iranshah Atash Behram.
  • Lakhpat, Kutch, is associated with Guru Nanak's travels.
  • Taranga is associated with Ajitanatha, the second Tirthankara.
  • Dev Ni Mori is an important Buddhist archaeological site near Shamlaji.

[References: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Chapter 6, Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, Section 7.2, p. 155; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Class 10, Social Science, English medium, 2020 reprint, Chapters 3 and 6, pp. 25–26, 49–50; District Kutch, Haji Pir Dargah and Lakhpat; Gujarat Tourism, Sarkhej Roza, Udvada, Lakhpat, Taranga Hill and Dev Ni Mori; District Devbhumi Dwarka, Places of Interest; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, Palitana and Shatrunjaya Hill; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Six Gujarat heritage sites matched to their religious traditions, highlighting Haji Pir Dargah as a shared Hindu-Muslim pilgrimage shrine.
pictures.caption: Gujarat's diverse religious heritage.

title: Multi-Faith Pilgrimage Sites and Religious Heritage of Gujarat

body:
Pilgrimage centres and their distinguishing identities

The major pilgrimage centres of Gujarat can be distinguished by their geographical locations, principal religious associations and characteristic sacred features. These attributes are especially useful when evaluating correctly and incorrectly matched pairs.

CentreDistrictPrincipal associationDistinctive feature
DwarkaDevbhumi DwarkaKrishnaWestern Char Dham
SomnathGir SomnathShivaJyotirlinga
AmbajiBanaskanthaArasuri AmbaVisa Yantra and Gabbar Hill
PalitanaBhavnagarAdinathaShatrunjaya Hill
GirnarJunagadhNeminatha; Hindu shrinesLili Parikrama
DakorKhedaKrishna as RanchhodraiGomti Lake
PavagadhPanchmahalKalika MataChampaner-Pavagadh World Heritage property

Religious classifications that must remain distinct

A Char Dham destination belongs to the traditional network of 4 major Hindu pilgrimage centres. Dwarka is Gujarat's representative in this network.

A Jyotirlinga belongs to the traditional group of 12 especially sacred Shiva shrines. Somnath and Nageshwar are the Gujarat examples.

A Shakti Peetha is associated with worship of the Divine Mother and traditions concerning Sati. Ambaji and Pavagadh belong to this category.

A Jain tirtha is a sacred pilgrimage centre associated with Jain religious traditions and spiritual teachers. Palitana, Girnar and Taranga are important Gujarat examples.

Important Tirthankara associations

TirthankaraTraditional numberGujarat pilgrimage centre
Adinatha or Rishabhanatha1stPalitana
Ajitanatha2ndTaranga
Neminatha or Arishtanemi22ndGirnar

Festivals and pilgrimage observances

Several pilgrimage centres are associated with distinctive annual religious gatherings. The names of these gatherings often provide a direct clue to their associated places.

  • Janmashtami: Particularly significant at Dwarka because of Krishna worship.
  • Falgun Purnima: Particularly associated with the Ranchhodraiji pilgrimage at Dakor.
  • Bhadarvi Poonam: The major annual pilgrimage gathering at Ambaji.
  • Kartik Purnima: Marks the conclusion of Chaturmas and the reopening of the Shatrunjaya pilgrimage season.
  • Lili Parikrama: The circumambulation around Girnar during the bright fortnight of Kartik.
  • Mahashivratri: Particularly associated with Somnath and the Bhavnath Mahadev Fair at Girnar.
  • Navratri: Particularly significant at Shakti pilgrimage centres such as Ambaji and Pavagadh.

These associations identify especially important observances. They do not establish that a particular festival is celebrated exclusively at one site.

Essential chronological associations

Year or periodEvent
1025–1026 CEMahmud of Ghazni's raid on Somnath
1484 CEMahmud Begada's capture of Pavagadh
1536 CEEnd of Champaner's period as the capital of Gujarat
1772 CEConstruction of the present Ranchhodraiji Temple at Dakor
1947Post-independence initiative to reconstruct Somnath
11 May 1951Consecration of the Jyotirlinga in the reconstructed Somnath Temple
2004UNESCO inscription of Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park

Recognising different kinds of sacred geography

Dwarka and Somnath are coastal religious centres. Dakor is associated with a sacred lake. Ambaji, Palitana, Girnar and Pavagadh demonstrate the importance of hills and mountains within pilgrimage traditions.

Natural features may themselves become objects of religious significance or provide the setting for religious journeys. Ritual bathing at a sacred waterfront, climbing a temple hill and circumambulating a mountain are therefore different expressions of pilgrimage.

Prelims focus

  • Dwarka and Dakor share Krishna worship but have different geographical and institutional identities.
  • Somnath and Nageshwar are Shiva Jyotirlingas.
  • Ambaji and Pavagadh belong to the Shakti Peetha tradition.
  • Palitana, Taranga and Girnar are associated with the 1st, 2nd and 22nd Tirthankaras respectively.
  • Girnar and Champaner-Pavagadh contain heritage associated with several religious traditions.
  • Trap: Religious classification, geographical location, architectural style and UNESCO recognition are separate attributes of a heritage site.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Class 10, Social Science, English medium, 2020 reprint, Chapter 6, pp. 49–50; NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Chapter 6, pp. 94–95; Gujarat Tourism, Religious Sites and individual pilgrimage-site descriptions; official websites of the districts of Devbhumi Dwarka, Gir Somnath, Banaskantha, Junagadh, Kheda and Panchmahal; Shri Ranchhodraiji Maharaj Mandir, About the Temple; Shree Somnath Trust, About Us; Ministry of Tourism, Utsav, Girnar Lili Parikrama; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park, List No. 1101; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
